title: After last year's storm, this remote Alaska town is still picking up the pieces
summary: In October 2025, the remnants of a typhoon seriously damaged Alaska Native villages in the far western part of the state. A year later, one of the hardest hit communities is still recovering.

Weather After last year's storm, this remote Alaska town is still picking up the pieces October 31, 2026 5:00 AM ET By Samantha Watson Construction crews work on houses and other building throughout Kipnuk after ex-typhoon Halong hit Alaska's coast in October of 2025. Gabby Hiestand Salgado/KYUK hide caption toggle caption i Gabby Hiestand Salgado/KYUK Last fall , the remnants of Typhoon Halong tore through numerous small Alaska Native villages off the road system in Western Alaska. The storm destroyed infrastructure, floated homes off their foundations, and displaced over a thousand people. A year later, hundreds remain displaced as the slow work of repair in a remote part of the state continues. And in one of the hardest hit communities – the small town of Kipnuk – people still aren't sure when they'll be moving back. Sponsor Message Environment What we know about the devastating storm in Western Alaska 'Working as fast as we can' The village of under 200 homes is situated on the wide open tundra and only consistently accessible by plane. A year ago, 90% of the residences here were damaged by the remnants of Typhoon Halong, according to the State of Alaska's Emergency Operations Center. Dozens were swept off their foundations, some with families still inside . The community is now largely scattered across Alaska – some outside the region their ancestors have lived in for thousands of years. Kipnuk 10 months after ex-typhoon Halong hit Alaska's coast in October of 2025. Gabby Hiestand Salgado/KYUK hide caption toggle caption i Gabby Hiestand Salgado/KYUK Throughout the past year, crews have been working on repairs. On a clear day in August, Eddie Chuckwuk's construction crew attempted what sounded like magic: raising a building back onto its foundations using air compressors. Only on NPR Archaeologists are racing to save precious artifacts in Alaska after last year's storm Chuckwuk is one of several dozen people who have been working long days to rebuild the place where he grew up. " We're working as fast as possible as we can to get the people back in town," Chuckwuk says. "That's what I just want to see – for everybody to come back and enjoy where they grew up instead of being placed in a different place … where they're not used to. It's pretty hard." Workers helping clear debris from the tundra around Kipnuk and construction crews working on houses 10 months after ex-typhoon Halong hit Alaska's coast in October of 2025. Gabby Hiestand Salgado/KYUK hide caption toggle caption i Gabby Hiestand Salgado/KYUK Challenges remain in moving back This work is critical to getting Kipnuk's homes in shape to live in again, but the town is far from being fully restored. Sponsor Message According to the state, most people in Kipnuk didn't have home or flood insurance. They estimate that funds from the Federal Emergency Management Agency will make most of the homes livable by Thanksgiving – meaning replacing wet insulation and repairing windows, doors and roofs. But the funds won't be enough to return some severely damaged homes to how they were before the storm. The state is currently appealing for additional funding to build replacement housing. Only on NPR People's houses are collapsing into the ocean. FEMA gives them no other option There's also no estimate on when the school will reopen. Leona Paul, who has been working as a cook to feed the construction teams, says even if the houses are habitable, some people were too traumatized by the storm to return. "I think it's too overwhelming for them," she says, "especially the older people." Climate Houses floated away in this Alaska Native village. Now residents want to move And climate change is making towns like Kipnuk more vulnerable to future storms . Most people in town want to rebuild the village somewhere safer but the funding they have received so far from FEMA can only go towards restoring what was damaged . Kipnuk hasn't yet found the money to move. In August, damage from the October 2025 storm was still visible in Kipnuk. Gabby Hiestand Salgado/KYUK hide caption toggle caption i Gabby Hiestand Salgado/KYUK Living away from home takes a toll Right now residents may not have a better option other than moving back. Many say living in bigger towns, or cities like Anchorage, has been tough. People aren't speaking as much Yugtun – the native language. They're farther from loved ones. Their kids, who are used to playing all over town, have to watch out for cars. Leona Paul, who spent part of the summer in Kipnuk, says she likes being there .
